plugin.name: Anxiety Aid Tools
plugin.description: Guided calm practices around your pet, starting with breathing and muscle relaxation. The OpenPets companion of https://anxietyaidtools.com/.
command.startPmr.description: Start a progressive muscle relaxation session.
command.startGuided.description: Start guided breathing with your last pattern.
session.title: Breathing
session.subtitle: Anxiety Aid Tools
pattern.name: Calm 4-6
phase.in.label: Breathe in slowly
phase.out.label: Breathe out slowly
guided.session.title: Guided breathing
guided.session.subtitle: Anxiety Aid Tools
guided.pattern.box.name: Box
guided.pattern.box.heading: Box breathing · 4-4-4-4
guided.pattern.box.body: Four equal counts: in, hold, out, hold. The even structure gives your attention something steady to follow when your thoughts are racing or you need to stay composed under pressure.
guided.pattern.box.detail: Best for: focus, concentration, staying composed
guided.pattern.calming.name: Calming
guided.pattern.calming.heading: Calming · 4-7-8
guided.pattern.calming.body: A short inhale, a long hold, and an even longer exhale. The eight-count out-breath is what slows you down. Four rounds is a common place to start; if the seven-count hold feels like a strain, shorten it.
guided.pattern.calming.detail: Best for: anxiety relief, winding down, sleep
guided.pattern.energizing.name: Energizing
guided.pattern.energizing.heading: Energizing · 4-4-6
guided.pattern.energizing.body: A balanced rhythm with a slightly longer exhale. It steadies you without making you drowsy, which suits the middle of a working day.
guided.pattern.energizing.detail: Best for: mental clarity, energy, a midday reset
guided.pattern.quick.name: Quick reset
guided.pattern.quick.heading: Quick reset · 3-3-3
guided.pattern.quick.body: Short, even counts you can finish in under a minute. Useful when there is no time for a full session but you want to interrupt a spike of stress.
guided.pattern.quick.detail: Best for: quick stress relief, busy moments
guided.info.intro: Breathing patterns for different moments. Pick one and follow the orb: it grows as you breathe in, stays still while you hold, and settles as you breathe out.
guided.info.patterns.heading: The patterns
guided.info.patterns.body: Switch between them on the card at any time, even mid-session.
guided.info.how.body: Following a set count turns an automatic process into something you steer. Slow, paced breathing shifts the nervous system toward its calming branch, and the counting gives an anxious mind one concrete thing to do. Different ratios suit different moments: even counts for focus, a longer exhale for winding down, short counts for a quick reset.
guided.info.how.card1.title: Rhythmic control
guided.info.how.card1.body: A fixed count gives your attention an anchor while your breathing slows.
guided.info.how.card2.title: Pattern variety
guided.info.how.card2.body: Even timing supports focus, a longer exhale deepens relaxation, and short patterns fit into a minute.
guided.info.how.card3.title: Nervous system
guided.info.how.card3.body: Slow breathing engages the vagus nerve, which helps bring down heart rate and the body's stress response.
guided.info.when.item1: When you feel anxious or overwhelmed and want something to hold on to
guided.info.when.item2: Before sleep, to quiet racing thoughts
guided.info.when.item3: Before a stressful meeting, call, or event
guided.info.when.item4: Every day, to build a steadier baseline
guided.info.tips.card1.title: One pattern at a time
guided.info.tips.card1.body: Stay with one pattern for a week or so before switching. Familiarity makes it easier to reach for when you need it.
guided.info.tips.card2.title: Comfortable seat
guided.info.tips.card2.body: Sit with your back supported and shoulders loose. Breathe through your nose if you can.
guided.info.tips.card3.title: Ease off the holds
guided.info.tips.card3.body: Holds should feel gentle, never strained. If you feel light-headed, drop the holds and breathe normally.
guided.info.disclaimer: This is a breathing practice for everyday calm. It is not therapy and does not treat anxiety disorders or any medical condition. If you feel dizzy or light-headed, skip the holds and breathe normally. If you are pregnant or have a heart or lung condition, check with a clinician before practicing breath holds.
grounding.session.title: Grounding 5-4-3-2-1
grounding.session.subtitle: Anxiety Aid Tools
grounding.see.label: See
grounding.see.title: Look around you
grounding.see.item1.text: Something with an interesting color or pattern
grounding.see.item1.guidance: Look for textures, reflections, or colors that catch your eye.
grounding.see.item2.text: An object with a smooth surface
grounding.see.item2.guidance: Notice how light hits it: glossy, matte, or somewhere in between?
grounding.see.item3.guidance: Watch how light and shadow shift.
grounding.see.item4.text: A detail you hadn't noticed before
grounding.see.item5.guidance: Notice what makes it comforting: its color, its shape, or a memory.
grounding.touch.label: Feel
grounding.touch.title: Feel around you
grounding.touch.prompt: Find 4 things you can touch or feel
grounding.touch.item1.guidance: Is it warm, cool, or neutral? Notice it on your hands and face.
grounding.touch.item2.guidance: Feel the fabric between your fingers: soft, rough, or smooth?
grounding.touch.item3.text: What you're sitting or standing on
grounding.touch.item3.guidance: Press into it a little. Is it firm, soft, warm, or cool?
grounding.touch.item4.guidance: Run your fingers over it and notice the texture.
grounding.hear.label: Hear
grounding.hear.title: Listen carefully
grounding.hear.item1.guidance: Close your eyes for a moment and listen inward.
grounding.hear.item2.guidance: Traffic, birds, voices: what can you pick out beyond the room?
grounding.hear.item3.text: A quiet sound you usually ignore
grounding.hear.item3.guidance: A hum, a fan, air moving, the building settling.
grounding.smell.label: Smell
grounding.smell.title: Take a breath
grounding.smell.item1.guidance: Breathe in slowly. Is it fresh, stale, scented, or neutral?
grounding.smell.item2.guidance: Coffee, soap, fabric, or your own sleeve.
grounding.taste.label: Taste
grounding.taste.title: Notice the taste
grounding.taste.item1.text: The taste in your mouth right now
grounding.taste.item1.guidance: Sweet, salty, minty, or neutral? A sip of water counts too.
grounding.info.intro: A way to step out of spiraling thoughts by noticing what is actually around you. Move through your senses at your own pace: five things you see, four you feel, three you hear, two you smell, one you taste.
grounding.info.how.body: When anxiety spikes, attention narrows onto the threat and the thoughts about it. Naming concrete things you can see, feel, hear, smell, and taste pulls attention back to the room you are in. The countdown gives your mind a simple, finite task, which is hard to do while also spiraling. There is no right answer: noticing is the whole exercise.
grounding.info.how.card1.title: Sensory focus
grounding.info.how.card1.body: Deliberately using your senses gives attention something real and immediate to hold, instead of worries about what might happen.
grounding.info.how.card2.title: A simple task
grounding.info.how.card2.body: Counting down from five is easy to follow even when thinking feels hard, and it has a clear end.
grounding.info.how.card3.title: Back to the present
grounding.info.how.card3.body: Concrete details root you in the here and now, which interrupts rumination about the past or the future.
grounding.info.science.body: Grounding is a standard skill in cognitive-behavioral, dialectical-behavior, and trauma-focused therapy, taught for panic, overwhelm, and dissociation. Studies of the 5-4-3-2-1 exercise on its own are still scarce: the research below includes sensory grounding or closely related present-moment practice as part of wider programs, so read it as support for the approach rather than proof of this one exercise.
grounding.info.science.card1.title: Children with Tourette syndrome
grounding.info.science.card1.body: In a 2025 randomized trial with 121 children, a 12-week mindfulness program built on breathwork, body awareness, and sensory grounding reduced anxiety, especially separation and social anxiety.
grounding.info.science.card2.title: Functional neurological disorder
grounding.info.science.card2.body: An outpatient clinic taught the 5-4-3-2-1 exercise among its self-management skills for sensory overload; patients' mental-health and functioning scores improved after treatment.
grounding.info.science.card3.title: A shared therapy tool
grounding.info.science.card3.body: A 2021 review of evidence-based psychotherapies for functional neurological disorders lists sensory grounding as a tool shared across several different treatment approaches.
grounding.info.when.item1: During a panic spike or a wave of acute anxiety
grounding.info.when.item2: When you feel overwhelmed, foggy, or disconnected from your surroundings
grounding.info.when.item3: Before a stressful event, to steady yourself first
grounding.info.when.item4: After a trigger or a flashback, to come back to the present
grounding.info.notice.item1: Racing thoughts slowing within a minute or two
grounding.info.notice.item2: Your breathing and heart rate settling
grounding.info.notice.item3: Clearer thinking, so you can respond instead of react
grounding.info.notice.item4: More confidence that you can steady yourself next time
grounding.info.tips.card1.title: Go slow
grounding.info.tips.card1.body: Spend a few seconds on each thing you notice. Rushing turns it into a checklist instead of a pause.
grounding.info.tips.card2.title: Be specific
grounding.info.tips.card2.body: Instead of "a chair", try "a wooden chair with a worn red cushion". Detail holds attention better.
grounding.info.tips.card3.title: Repeat if needed
grounding.info.tips.card3.body: If the anxiety comes back, go around again. You can do as many rounds as you need.
grounding.info.disclaimer: Grounding is a self-help skill for everyday calm. It is not therapy and does not treat anxiety disorders, trauma, or any medical condition. If you are in crisis or feel unsafe, contact local emergency services or a crisis line.
meditation.session.title: Guided meditation
meditation.session.subtitle: Anxiety Aid Tools
meditation.physiological-sigh-reset.abou: Two short inhales, one long exhale, repeated. A quick way to take the edge off a stress spike.
meditation.structural-realignment-protoc: A slow scan from feet to forehead that looks for held tension and lets it go.
meditation.kinetic-grounding-sequence.ab: A walking practice: steps paced with the breath, attention on your feet meeting the ground.
meditation.hypnagogic-induction-sequence: A lying-down wind-down that settles attention on the senses and the weight of the body before sleep.
meditation.vagus-nerve-delta-descent.abo: Long exhales and a soft hum, lying down. Made for the last minutes before sleep.
meditation.oceanic-consciousness-project: A visualization of resting deep beneath the ocean, watching thoughts pass like waves on the surface.
meditation.infinite-horizon-projection.a: A visualization that widens attention to a calm, open horizon so worries feel smaller.
meditation.metta-loving-kindness-protoco: Loving-kindness: silent phrases of goodwill for yourself, someone you care about, then everyone.
meditation.info.intro: Narrated sessions from Anxiety Aid Tools. Pick one, press play, and follow the voice. You can pause, go back 15 seconds, or skip a part whenever you like.
meditation.info.grounded.heading: For stress, body, and sleep
meditation.info.spiritual.heading: For wider awareness
meditation.info.how.body: Guided meditation gives your attention one thing to follow: a voice, the breath, a part of the body, an image. When the mind wanders, and it will, the guidance brings it back. Over time, that practice of noticing and returning makes it easier to step out of anxious loops in daily life.
meditation.info.how.card1.title: An anchor for attention
meditation.info.how.card1.body: Following one voice and one sensation leaves less room for spiraling thoughts.
meditation.info.how.card2.title: The body settles
meditation.info.how.card2.body: Slow breathing and relaxed muscles shift the body away from the stress response.
meditation.info.how.card3.title: A skill that grows
meditation.info.how.card3.body: Noticing a wandering mind and coming back is the practice itself, and it gets easier with repetition.
meditation.info.science.body: Meditation has been studied in many randomized trials. Reviews find moderate reductions in anxiety and stress with regular practice, similar in size to other psychological approaches. The sessions here are short practices for everyday calm, not a treatment program.
meditation.info.science.card1.title: Meditation programs
meditation.info.science.card1.body: A 2014 review of 47 randomized trials found moderate evidence that mindfulness meditation programs improve anxiety and depression.
meditation.info.science.card2.title: Mindfulness-based therapy
meditation.info.science.card2.body: A 2010 meta-analysis of 39 studies found that mindfulness-based therapy moderately reduced anxiety, with larger effects in people with anxiety disorders.
meditation.info.science.card3.title: Loving-kindness
meditation.info.science.card3.body: A 2011 review describes how loving-kindness and compassion meditation increase positive emotions and reduce negative emotions and self-criticism.
meditation.info.when.item1: When your mind is busy and you want something to follow
meditation.info.when.item2: Before sleep, with the sleep sessions
meditation.info.when.item3: During a break, to reset between tasks
meditation.info.when.item4: Every day, as a short habit
meditation.info.tips.card1.title: Use headphones
meditation.info.tips.card1.body: A voice close to your ears is easier to follow and blocks out background noise.
meditation.info.tips.card2.title: Get comfortable
meditation.info.tips.card2.body: Sit or lie down as the session suggests. For the walking session, choose a safe, clear path.
meditation.info.tips.card3.title: Let the mind wander
meditation.info.tips.card3.body: Drifting off is normal. Each time you notice it, come back to the voice; that is the practice.
meditation.info.disclaimer: These sessions support everyday calm. They are not therapy and do not treat anxiety disorders or any medical condition. Do not listen to the sleep sessions while driving. If a practice brings up distress, stop and return to normal breathing.
meditation.physiological-sigh-reset.capt: Find a comfortable seated or lying position. Keep your spine relatively straight but not rigid.
The physiological sigh is a specific breathing pattern: two short inhales followed by one long exhale.
Take a deep breath in through your nose... and then another short, sharp inhale at the very top to fully expand the lungs.
Now, release a long, slow exhale through your mouth, as if you are sighing. Feel the tension leaving your shoulders.
Repeat this cycle. Inhale... inhale again... then a long, controlled sigh out.
Notice the immediate shift in your heart rate and the clarity returning to your mind.
Continue for a few more cycles, focusing purely on the mechanical rhythm of the breath.
meditation.structural-realignment-protoc: Begin by standing or sitting with your back supported. If standing, keep your feet hip-width apart and your knees slightly unlocked.
Close your eyes or fix your gaze on a single point in front of you. We are going to perform a structural audit of your current physical state.
Bring your awareness to your feet. Notice if you are gripping the floor with your toes or leaning too far in one direction. Allow your weight to distribute evenly.
Moving up to the knees. Ensure they aren't locked. Micro-bend them to allow the blood and energy to flow freely through the legs.
Now, check the pelvis. Is it tilted forward or back? Imagine a bowl of water at your center; try to keep it perfectly level.
Scan your abdomen. Are you holding your breath or pulling your stomach in? Let the belly soften. Let it move naturally with each breath.
To the ribcage and chest. Notice any 'bracing' or 'armoring.' Gently lift the sternum a fraction of an inch and feel the lungs expand without effort.
Notice your shoulders. They often creep toward the ears when we are in a high-arousal state. Drop them completely. Let them hang like heavy weights.
Now, the jaw. A primary site for stored stress. Separate your teeth slightly. Let your tongue rest behind your lower teeth.
Finally, the space between your eyebrows. Smooth it out. Imagine the skin on your forehead becoming tight and calm.
With the bracing removed, take three deep, slow breaths. Notice the structural integrity of your body when it is not holding tension.
Stay in this realigned state for a moment. Feel the difference between forced posture and easeful alignment.
Slowly open your eyes and carry this sense of physical openness back into your day.
meditation.kinetic-grounding-sequence.ca: Begin walking at a slow, deliberate pace. If you are already moving, slightly reduce your speed to bring full attention to the mechanics of your gait.
Adjust your posture. Imagine a string pulling the crown of your head toward the sky, while your shoulders drop completely, heavy and relaxed.
Now, bring your awareness to your feet. Feel the specific moment your heel makes contact with the ground. Notice the roll through the arch to the toes.
We will now synchronize your breath with your steps. Inhale for two steps, and exhale for four. Left, right, inhale... Left, right, left, right, exhale.
Focus on the pressure of the floor against your soles. With each step, imagine you are pushing the Earth away from you, feeling the stability of the ground beneath.
As you walk, allow your gaze to soften. Don't look at your feet; look ahead, allowing the world to flow past you in your peripheral vision.
Notice the weight of your arms swinging naturally. Feel the air moving against your skin. You are fully anchored in the physical reality of movement.
Continue this rhythm. Two steps in, four steps out. Heavy heels. Soft gaze. Deeply grounded in the present moment.
If your mind wanders, gently return to the sensation of your heels striking the ground. The floor is your primary anchor.
Slowly allow your breath to return to its natural rhythm while maintaining the awareness of your physical presence. Your sequence is complete.
meditation.hypnagogic-induction-sequence: Ensure you are lying in your preferred sleep position. Adjust your covers and pillows to minimize any physical feedback from your environment.
Close your eyes. We are beginning a protocol to lower your cognitive arousal and transition your brain toward the hypnagogic state.
Take three slow, deep breaths. On each exhale, imagine your body becoming heavier, and more fully supported by the surface beneath you.
Bring your attention to the backs of your eyelids. Even with your eyes closed, notice any faint patterns of light or shadow. Do not try to analyze them. Just observe.
We will now begin a 'sensory audit'. Notice the sensation of the air on your skin. Is it cool? Warm? Simply register the temperature without judgment.
Shift your attention to the sounds in your immediate environment. The furthest sound you can hear... and then the closest sound... the sound of your own breathing.
Now, we will engage in 'micro-visualization'. Briefly visualize a neutral object-a smooth stone, a clear glass of water, or a single leaf. Hold it for a moment, then let it dissolve.
If your mind begins to loop on active thoughts or future tasks, gently acknowledge the 'active' mode and redirect your focus back to the weight of your limbs.
Notice the feeling of your heels, your calves, and your thighs pressing into the bed. Feel the gravity acting on your body, pulling you into a state of deep rest.
Your breathing is now automatic. You are not controlling it. You are simply observing the mechanical rise and fall of your chest.
As your thoughts become more fragmented and dream-like, allow them to drift. Do not try to hold onto any specific sequence of logic.
You are now entering the transition. The boundary between wakefulness and sleep is thinning. Allow yourself to be pulled into the stillness.
Rest in this state of deepening neutrality. Sleep is a natural biological function that your body knows how to perform. Let it take over.
meditation.vagus-nerve-delta-descent.cap: Prepare for rest by lying flat on your back, arms slightly away from your body, palms facing upward.
Close your eyes gently. We are beginning a protocol to down-regulate your nervous system by targeting the vagus nerve.
Bring your attention to your breath. Don't change it yet, just observe the natural rise and fall of your chest.
We will now begin the 'Extended Exhale' rhythm. Inhale for a count of four... then exhale slowly through pursed lips for a count of eight.
Inhale... one, two, three, four. Exhale... one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. Feel your heart rate begin to settle.
With each long exhale, imagine your body sinking deeper into the surface beneath you. Total weight, total release.
Next, we add a gentle sub-vocal hum. During your long exhale, create a low-frequency vibration at the back of your throat. Mmmmmm.
This vibration physically stimulates the vagal fibers in your throat, sending a direct signal to your brain that you are safe and it is time to rest.
Inhale deeply... and hum softy as you exhale... feeling the resonance in your chest and skull.
Let the hum fade into silence, but continue the rhythm. Inhale for four... exhale for eight.
Notice any remaining tension in your jaw or forehead. Let it dissolve with the next breath.
Your nervous system is now in a state of 'delta descent.' The parasympathetic system is fully engaged.
Continue this rhythm on your own. Each exhale is a surrender to sleep.
The body is heavy. The mind is quiet. Sleep is now the natural next step.
meditation.oceanic-consciousness-project: Close your eyes and take a slow, deep breath. Feel the boundaries of your body beginning to soften.
Imagine yourself at the edge of a vast, infinite ocean. The water is deep, dark indigo, reflecting a sky filled with stars.
Step into the water. As you do, notice that you don't feel cold or wet-only a sense of becoming one with the deep.
Descend slowly beneath the surface. Leave the sounds and chaos of the world above. Here, everything is still.
Look up at the surface from far below. You see waves-ripples of light and motion. These are your thoughts.
Notice a wave of worry... a wave of memory... a wave of planning. They move across the surface, far above you.
You are not the waves. You are the vast, silent depth beneath them. Infinite. Unshakable.
Feel the pressure of the deep water as a gentle, cosmic hug. It holds you in perfect stillness.
There is no 'you' and 'ocean'. There is only the vastness. Any border between your mind and the infinite is dissolving.
Rest in this sapphire silence. Let your awareness expand until it touches the very floor of the cosmos.
When you are ready, slowly begin to rise. Carry the stillness of the deep back to the surface of your conscious mind.
Gently open your eyes, keeping that sense of oceanic depth within you as you return to the room.
meditation.infinite-horizon-projection.c: Settle into a posture that feels both stable and effortless. Close your eyes and let your breathing adopt a natural, unforced rhythm.
Scan your body briefly, not to change anything, but to acknowledge your starting point. Feel the weight of your limbs and the contact of your body with the surface beneath you.
Now, imagine a thin line of light appearing in the far distance of your internal vision. This is the horizon of your awareness.
Gently begin to project your sense of 'self' toward that line. Imagine yourself moving away from the immediate sensations of the body, toward the vast, open space ahead.
As you approach this horizon, notice that it is not a boundary, but an infinite expanse. It is perfectly still, silent, and deeply peaceful.
You are no longer defined by your thoughts or the physical boundaries of your skin. You are the vast space in which these things arise.
From this perspective, look back at your current stressors or anxieties. See them as small, flickering lights in an infinite night. They are present, but they are not the whole picture.
Rest here in the infinite horizon. There is nowhere to go, nothing to fix, and no one you need to be. Just pure, expansive presence.
Notice the profound quiet that exists at the center of this expansion. This stillness is always available to you, regardless of the noise of daily life.
Slowly, begin to draw your awareness back toward the center of your chest. Carry the scale and quiet of the horizon with you.
Feel the weight of your body again, but notice the new sense of spaciousness within. When you are ready, gently open your eyes.
meditation.metta-loving-kindness-protoco: Find a comfortable seated position. Let your hands rest gently in your lap or on your knees. Close your eyes or soften your gaze.
Take three slow, deep breaths. With each exhale, allow any tension in your shoulders and jaw to release.
Bring your attention to the center of your chest-your heart space. Imagine a small, warm light glowing there.
We will now begin directing phrases of loving-kindness inward. Repeat silently after each phrase: May I be happy.
May I be healthy. Feel the sincerity of the wish, even if it feels unfamiliar.
May I be safe from inner and outer harm. Let each phrase land gently, without forcing any emotion.
May I live with ease and peace. Notice any shift in the quality of the warmth in your chest.
Now, bring to mind someone you care about-a friend, family member, or mentor. See their face clearly in your mind.
Direct the same phrases toward them: May you be happy. May you be healthy. May you be safe. May you live with ease.
Expand this circle of kindness outward. Imagine it spreading beyond this room, to your neighborhood, your city, and eventually to all beings everywhere.
May all beings be happy. May all beings be healthy. May all beings be safe. May all beings live with ease.
Rest in this feeling of expansive warmth. When you are ready, take a deep breath and gently open your eyes, carrying this kindness with you.
visualization.session.title: Peaceful visualization
visualization.session.subtitle: Anxiety Aid Tools
visualization.info.intro: Narrated journeys to calm places: a mountain at sunrise, a forest grove, a rainy cabin. Pick a scene, close your eyes if you like, and let the voice paint it.
visualization.info.how.body: Imagining a calm place in detail, with its colors, sounds, smells, and textures, gives the mind something peaceful to hold instead of worry. The body tends to follow: breathing slows and muscles loosen. With practice, the scene becomes a place you can return to quickly when stress rises.
visualization.info.how.card1.title: A calm place to hold
visualization.info.how.card1.body: A detailed, peaceful scene takes up the attention that worry would otherwise fill.
visualization.info.how.card2.title: All the senses
visualization.info.how.card2.body: Sounds, smells, and textures make the scene more vivid and the relaxation deeper.
visualization.info.how.card3.title: Easier each time
visualization.info.how.card3.body: Revisiting the same scene makes it faster to call up when you need it.
visualization.info.science.body: Guided imagery has mostly been studied in medical settings, such as before surgery or in hospital. Small randomized trials find lower anxiety after imagery sessions. The evidence is encouraging but limited; treat these scenes as a way to rest, not a treatment.
visualization.info.science.card1.title: In hospital
visualization.info.science.card1.body: A 2021 randomized trial in patients with COVID-19 found that guided imagery sessions lowered anxiety and muscle pain compared with usual care.
visualization.info.science.card2.title: Before surgery
visualization.info.science.card2.body: A 2015 randomized trial in joint replacement patients found that structured touch combined with guided imagery reduced anxiety and pain.
visualization.info.science.card3.title: Generalized anxiety
visualization.info.science.card3.body: A small 2023 study of guided imagery in people with generalized anxiety disorder reported lower anxiety and better quality of life after the sessions.
visualization.info.when.item1: When worry keeps looping and you want a break from it
visualization.info.when.item2: Before sleep, with the evening and night scenes
visualization.info.when.item3: Before a stressful appointment or event
visualization.info.when.item4: Any time you want a few minutes somewhere calmer
visualization.info.tips.card1.title: Use headphones
visualization.info.tips.card1.body: The narration is easier to sink into with the world turned down.
visualization.info.tips.card2.title: Fill in the details
visualization.info.tips.card2.body: Add your own colors, sounds, and smells. There is no wrong way to picture the scene.
visualization.info.tips.card3.title: Make it yours
visualization.info.tips.card3.body: Return to the scene that works best for you; familiarity makes it faster to reach calm.
visualization.info.disclaimer: These scenes support everyday calm. They are not therapy and do not treat anxiety disorders or any medical condition. Do not listen while driving. If a scene brings up distress, open your eyes and return to normal breathing.
visualization.mountainPeakSunrise.title: Mountain Peak Sunrise
visualization.mountainPeakSunrise.captio: You find yourself standing on a peaceful mountain peak, the world spread out before you like a beautiful painting.
The sunrise paints the sky in gentle colors - soft pinks, warm oranges, and golden yellows stretching across the horizon.
Cool, fresh mountain air fills your lungs. Each breath is pure and energizing, washing away any tension or worry.
Below you, layers of mountains roll into the distance like sleeping giants, covered in a soft morning mist.
You feel completely safe here, standing on solid ground, connected to the earth beneath your feet.
The sun's gentle warmth touches your face, filling you with peace and quiet strength.
This is your peaceful place - you can return here anytime by simply closing your eyes and remembering this moment.
visualization.tranquilForestGrove.title: Tranquil Forest Grove
visualization.tranquilForestGrove.captio: You're walking into a beautiful forest clearing, where ancient trees create a natural cathedral around you.
Gentle sunlight filters through the leaves above, creating patterns of light and shadow on the forest floor.
The air here is filled with the fresh scent of growing things - moss, earth, and the clean smell of leaves.
Soft moss cushions your steps, and you can hear the peaceful sounds of birds singing and leaves rustling in the gentle breeze.
You settle beside a smooth tree trunk, feeling completely supported and safe in nature's embrace.
Every breath brings you deeper peace, as if the forest itself is sharing its ancient calm with you.
This grove is your sanctuary - a place where you can always find peace and renewal whenever you need it.
visualization.peacefulOceanBeach.title: Peaceful Ocean Beach
visualization.peacefulOceanBeach.caption: You're walking barefoot on a beautiful beach, feeling the warm, soft sand between your toes.
Gentle waves roll onto the shore in a peaceful rhythm, like the earth's own breathing, calm and steady.
The ocean stretches endlessly before you, its surface sparkling in the sunlight like scattered diamonds.
A warm, gentle breeze carries the clean scent of salt water and touches your skin with perfect comfort.
You find the perfect spot to rest, feeling completely at peace with the endless rhythm of the waves.
Each wave that rolls in takes away any stress or worry, carrying it out to sea where it dissolves completely.
This beach is your peaceful refuge - the waves will always be here, ready to wash away your cares whenever you return.
visualization.sereneGardenParadise.title: Serene Garden Paradise
visualization.sereneGardenParadise.capti: You enter a magnificent garden where every flower seems to welcome you with vibrant colors and gentle fragrances.
A small fountain creates the most peaceful sound as clear water flows over smooth stones in the center of the garden.
Soft petals create a living rainbow around you - deep purples, bright yellows, soft pinks.
The air is filled with natural perfumes, and everything feels warm and welcoming.
You find a comfortable place to rest among the flowers, feeling safe and loved by nature.
This garden grows more beautiful with each breath you take, as if responding to your peaceful presence.
This is your garden of peace - it will always be in bloom, waiting for you whenever you need beauty and calm.
visualization.starlitMeadowNight.title: Starlit Meadow Night
visualization.starlitMeadowNight.caption: You're lying comfortably in a soft meadow, looking up at a sky filled with sparkling stars.
The grass beneath you is perfectly soft, like nature's own cushion, supporting your body completely.
Above you, the Milky Way stretches across the heavens like a river of light, beautiful beyond description.
The night air is comfortable, with a gentle breeze that carries the sweet scent of night-blooming flowers.
You feel small in the best possible way - connected to something vast and peaceful that holds you safely.
Each star seems to shine just for you, sending down light that fills you with wonder and peace.
This meadow under the stars is your place of infinite calm - you can always look up and find peace in the vastness.
visualization.cozyRainyCabin.title: Cozy Rainy Cabin

visualization.cozyRainyCabin.caption2: Raindrops drum a gentle rhythm on the roof and trickle down the glass, creating the most soothing soundtrack.

visualization.cozyRainyCabin.caption5: A thick blanket rests across your legs, and you feel perfectly supported by the chair as your entire body unwinds.
visualization.cozyRainyCabin.caption6: You cradle a warm mug between your hands, letting the steam rise slowly toward your face as the rain continues to sing.
visualization.cozyRainyCabin.caption7: This cabin is your private refuge-whenever you need peace, you can return to this cozy, rain-kissed evening and rest here.
visualization.mistyLakesideDawn.title: Misty Lakeside Dawn

visualization.mistyLakesideDawn.caption2: Thin mist floats above the water, drifting lazily as dawn begins to color the sky.

visualization.mistyLakesideDawn.caption6: A distant loon calls once and the sound echoes softly before fading back into silence.
visualization.mistyLakesideDawn.caption7: This lakeside dawn belongs to you-return to it whenever you need calm, and the water will be waiting.

pmr.session.title: Muscle relaxation
pmr.session.subtitle: Anxiety Aid Tools
pmr.group.right-hand.name: Right Hand & Forearm
pmr.group.right-hand.tenseCue: Make a tight fist, squeeze hard, and feel the tension in your fingers and forearm.
pmr.group.right-hand.releaseCue: Open your hand, let it go completely limp, and feel your fingers relax.
pmr.group.left-hand.name: Left Hand & Forearm
pmr.group.left-hand.tenseCue: Make a tight fist, squeeze hard, and feel the tension in your fingers and forearm.
pmr.group.left-hand.releaseCue: Open your hand, let it go completely limp, and notice the warm, heavy feeling.
pmr.group.right-arm.name: Right Upper Arm
pmr.group.right-arm.tenseCue: Bend your elbow, flex your bicep hard, and feel the muscle bulge.
pmr.group.right-arm.releaseCue: Lower your arm to your side, let the muscle go soft, and feel the heaviness.
pmr.group.left-arm.name: Left Upper Arm
pmr.group.left-arm.tenseCue: Bend your elbow, flex your bicep hard, and feel the strength.
pmr.group.left-arm.releaseCue: Lower your arm to your side, let tension drain away, and feel the heaviness.
pmr.group.forehead.name: Forehead & Scalp
pmr.group.forehead.tenseCue: Raise your eyebrows high, wrinkle your forehead, and feel the tension across your scalp.
pmr.group.forehead.releaseCue: Let your eyebrows drop naturally, smooth out your forehead, and feel your skin relax.
pmr.group.face.name: Eyes & Nose
pmr.group.face.tenseCue: Squeeze your eyes tight, scrunch your nose up, and scrunch your whole face together.
pmr.group.face.releaseCue: Let your face go soft, eyes gently closed, nose and cheeks smooth and relaxed.
pmr.group.jaw.name: Mouth & Jaw
pmr.group.jaw.tenseCue: Bite down hard, clench your teeth, and feel your jaw muscles working.
pmr.group.jaw.releaseCue: Let your jaw drop slightly open, lips barely touching, and tongue resting softly.
pmr.group.neck.name: Neck & Throat
pmr.group.neck.tenseCue: Draw the chin in slightly and tighten the neck.
pmr.group.neck.releaseCue: Let your head find its natural position, neck long and loose, and throat open.
pmr.group.shoulders.name: Shoulders
pmr.group.shoulders.tenseCue: Pull your shoulders up high toward your ears and feel the squeeze in your upper back.
pmr.group.shoulders.releaseCue: Let your shoulders drop naturally, feeling them sink lower, heavy and loose.
pmr.group.upper-back.name: Upper Back & Chest
pmr.group.upper-back.tenseCue: Squeeze your shoulder blades together, arch your back slightly, and expand your chest.
pmr.group.upper-back.releaseCue: Let your back settle naturally, shoulder blades apart, and chest soft and open.
pmr.group.abdomen.name: Abdomen
pmr.group.abdomen.tenseCue: Tighten your abs hard, pull your belly button in, and make your stomach firm.
pmr.group.abdomen.releaseCue: Let your stomach go soft, breathe into your belly, and feel it rise and fall naturally.
pmr.group.lower-back.name: Lower Back
pmr.group.lower-back.tenseCue: Gently arch the lower back. Stop if it hurts.
pmr.group.lower-back.releaseCue: Let your back settle to its natural curve, supported, comfortable, and loose.
pmr.group.hips.name: Hips & Buttocks
pmr.group.hips.tenseCue: Squeeze your buttocks together hard, clench tight, and feel tension in your hips.
pmr.group.hips.releaseCue: Let your muscles go soft, feeling them spread naturally, heavy and relaxed.
pmr.group.right-thigh.name: Right Thigh
pmr.group.right-thigh.tenseCue: Straighten your right leg, flex your thigh muscle hard, and feel it firm and strong.
pmr.group.right-thigh.releaseCue: Let your leg rest naturally, thigh muscle soft, loose, heavy, and comfortable.
pmr.group.left-thigh.name: Left Thigh
pmr.group.left-thigh.tenseCue: Straighten your left leg, flex your thigh muscle hard, and feel the strength.
pmr.group.left-thigh.releaseCue: Let your leg rest naturally, thigh completely relaxed, and notice the contrast.
pmr.group.right-calf.name: Right Calf & Shin
pmr.group.right-calf.tenseCue: Point your foot down hard, then flex toes up toward your shin, feeling both sides work.
pmr.group.right-calf.releaseCue: Let your foot rest naturally, calf and shin completely loose and soft.
pmr.group.left-calf.name: Left Calf & Shin
pmr.group.left-calf.tenseCue: Point your foot down hard, then flex toes up toward your shin, feeling muscles engage.
pmr.group.left-calf.releaseCue: Let your foot rest naturally, all lower leg muscles relaxed and heavy.
pmr.group.right-foot.name: Right Foot
pmr.group.right-foot.tenseCue: Curl your toes down tight, scrunch them up, and feel tension in your foot arch.
pmr.group.right-foot.releaseCue: Let your toes uncurl naturally, foot completely soft, warm, and relaxed.
pmr.group.left-foot.name: Left Foot
pmr.group.left-foot.tenseCue: Curl your toes down tight, scrunch them up, and feel your arch working.
pmr.group.left-foot.releaseCue: Let your toes spread naturally, foot loose and relaxed, and all tension gone.
pmr.info.intro: Progressive muscle relaxation systematically releases physical tension throughout the body. Tense each muscle group firmly for 10 seconds, then release completely for 10 seconds to feel the contrast.
pmr.info.how.heading: How it works
pmr.info.how.body: Progressive muscle relaxation teaches your body the contrast between tension and relaxation. Deliberately tensing a muscle group and releasing it activates the parasympathetic nervous system, lowering heart rate and releasing built-up physical stress.
pmr.info.how.card1.title: Tension contrast
pmr.info.how.card1.body: Deliberately tensing muscles makes the subsequent release more noticeable and effective, releasing tension held without realizing it.
pmr.info.how.card2.title: Nervous system shift
pmr.info.how.card2.body: Releasing muscle tension triggers parasympathetic activation, slowing your heart rate and diminishing stress hormones.
pmr.info.how.card3.title: Body awareness
pmr.info.how.card3.body: Regular practice trains you to recognize physical tension earlier and release stress before it accumulates throughout your day.
pmr.info.science.heading: The science
pmr.info.science.body: Clinical trials show that progressive muscle relaxation produces significant, sustained reductions in anxiety across diverse settings, from high-stress hospital environments to academic performance.
pmr.info.science.card1.title: Clinical anxiety reduction
pmr.info.science.card1.body: A randomized trial found 30 minutes of daily progressive muscle relaxation over 5 days lowered anxiety scores by 22% compared to controls.
pmr.info.science.card2.title: Demanding environments
pmr.info.science.card2.body: In a randomized trial among 46 nurses, progressive muscle relaxation reduced anxiety on the DASS-21 with a large effect size (Cohen's d=1.61).
pmr.info.science.card3.title: Clinical training
pmr.info.science.card3.body: In 90 nursing students during clinical training, five 45-minute sessions reduced State-Trait Anxiety Inventory scores from 55 to 24.4 (a 56% decrease).
pmr.info.when.heading: When to practice
pmr.info.when.item1: When you notice physical tension building in shoulders, jaw, or back
pmr.info.when.item2: Before stressful events to release anticipatory tension
pmr.info.when.item3: At the end of your workday to transition into relaxation
pmr.info.when.item4: Before bed to release tension interfering with sleep
pmr.info.notice.heading: What you'll notice
pmr.info.notice.item1: Immediate awareness of tension you didn't realize you were holding
pmr.info.notice.item2: A deep sensation of warmth and heaviness as muscles release
pmr.info.notice.item3: Slower breathing and a calmer baseline heart rate
pmr.info.notice.item4: Faster ability to spot and release physical stress throughout the day
pmr.info.tips.heading: Tips for best results
pmr.info.tips.card1.title: Comfortable position
pmr.info.tips.card1.body: Sit in a supportive armchair or lie down comfortably. Loosen any tight clothing so your body is fully supported.
pmr.info.tips.card2.title: Gentle firmness
pmr.info.tips.card2.body: Tense each muscle firmly but never to the point of pain or cramping. The goal is clear sensation, not strain.
pmr.info.tips.card3.title: Notice the contrast
pmr.info.tips.card3.body: Focus your full attention on the difference between the tensed state and the limp release that follows.
pmr.info.disclaimer: This is a tension-and-release practice for everyday calm. It is not therapy and does not treat anxiety disorders or any medical condition. Tense firmly, not to the point of pain or cramping. If a movement hurts, skip that group. Stop if you feel dizzy or unwell.
info.intro: A short, guided breathing practice. Follow the orb: it grows as you breathe in and settles as you breathe out. You don't need to read any of this to start — it will be here whenever you're curious.
info.how.heading: How it works
info.how.body:
The 4:6 rhythm makes every exhale longer than the inhale. That long, slow out-breath stimulates the vagus nerve — the main pathway of the parasympathetic nervous system — signalling the body to shift from "fight or flight" into "rest and repair".

The shift is measurable: heart rate slows, blood pressure eases, and circulation improves, bringing more oxygen to the brain. Practised regularly, it becomes a reliable lever you can pull whenever stress builds.
info.how.card1.title: Vagal nerve activation
info.how.card1.body: Slow, deep breathing stimulates the vagus nerve, which connects the brain to the heart and digestive system and promotes a calm state.
info.how.card2.title: Optimal gas exchange
info.how.card2.body: Breathing at 4–6 breaths per minute optimizes oxygen delivery and CO₂ balance, countering the shallow over-breathing that often comes with anxiety.
info.how.card3.title: Lower stress hormones
info.how.card3.body: Regular practice reduces cortisol and other stress hormones, improving the body's baseline stress response over time.
info.science.heading: The science
info.science.body: Research consistently shows that slow, diaphragmatic breathing produces measurable reductions in anxiety, stress hormones, and physiological arousal. In one controlled study, an 8-week program of 15-minute sessions lowered negative affect and significantly decreased cortisol levels in healthy adults.
info.science.card1.title: Anxiety reduction
info.science.card1.body: Five days of guided deep breathing (15–20 minutes, four times daily) reduced anxiety scores in hospitalized patients by 43%, while a control group showed no change.
info.science.card2.title: Panic disorder
info.science.card2.body: A review of 16 studies found that slow-breathing training over 2–12 months reduced panic attack frequency and normalized CO₂ levels in panic disorder and agoraphobia.
info.science.card3.title: Generalized anxiety
info.science.card3.body: Three months of daily breathing practice reduced anxiety scores by 68% in a study of 41 people with generalized anxiety disorder.
info.when.heading: When to practice
info.when.item1: When you feel overwhelmed or stressed
info.when.item4: After stressful events, to reset your nervous system
info.notice.heading: What you'll notice
info.notice.item1: A calming effect within the first minute
info.notice.item3: A slower heart rate and softer muscle tension
info.notice.item4: Better stress resilience with regular practice
info.tips.heading: Tips for best results
info.tips.card1.title: Posture
info.tips.card1.body: Sit or stand tall so the lungs can expand fully. Keep the shoulders heavy and relaxed, not hunched.
info.tips.card2.title: Environment
info.tips.card2.body: Choose a quiet spot where you won't be interrupted. A comfortable temperature makes it easier to stay with the breath.
info.tips.card3.title: Consistency
info.tips.card3.body: Practice the same rhythm for a week before changing anything. Familiarity is what makes it work under real stress.
info.disclaimer: These exercises support everyday calm. They are not therapy and do not treat anxiety disorders or any medical condition. If a breathing exercise ever feels uncomfortable or makes you dizzy, stop and let your breath return to normal.
